messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 64
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Captivity
- Pcl5: 60

He is a 64-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life doing physical work, and he still speaks about himself as someone who is meant to “keep moving” and not make a fuss. Before the trauma, he is known in his family as steady and practical, the kind of husband who handles bills, repairs, and long shifts at the warehouse without complaint. He takes pride in providing for his wife and in being dependable, and he has little patience for anything he sees as weakness in himself.

The captivity begins while he is on a work-related trip years ago, when he is taken by men he does not know and held against his will for an extended period. He remembers the first hours most clearly: the shock of being separated from others, the loss of control, the strange split-second hope that this is a misunderstanding, and then the hard realization that it is not. In those early days, he stays alert to every sound, every change in footsteps, every shift in tone from his captors. He learns quickly that silence can be as threatening as shouting. He monitors the room for exits, but the place is designed to prevent escape, and the helplessness of that awareness settles deep in him.

During captivity, he survives by narrowing his attention to whatever is immediately in front of him. He counts time by meals, by lights on and off, by the ache in his joints, by the small routines he forces himself to maintain so he does not feel entirely erased. He tries not to think about his wife, because when he does, panic rises in his chest so sharply he feels he may choke on it. He is ashamed by how often his mind goes blank, how often fear leaves him feeling young and powerless. He tells himself to endure, to be patient, to stay alive long enough to return. That simple goal becomes the center of his world.

When he is eventually released, he returns home physically intact but changed in ways his family notices before he can name them. At first he is relieved to be in his own bed, to hear his wife moving in the kitchen, to sit at a familiar table. But even safety feels temporary. He checks doors and windows repeatedly. He sits with his back to the wall. He is startled by sudden noises, especially banging metal or voices raised in anger, and his body reacts before his mind can catch up. In the warehouse, where forklifts beep and pallets crash and men call across long aisles, he keeps scanning the space as if danger could appear at any moment. He becomes tense during shifts and finds himself calculating where to stand, who is near him, how quickly he could move if something went wrong.

At night, sleep does not bring relief. He wakes often, sometimes with no clear dream, only a sense of dread and a racing heart. Other times he dreams of being confined again, of hearing footsteps outside a locked door, of not being able to make himself heard. He avoids talking about what happened, even with his wife, because words feel like they might open the whole experience all over again. When family members ask questions, he answers briefly and changes the subject. He notices that he is more irritable than before, quicker to snap over small things, then deeply ashamed afterward. He does not like the man he has become in these moments, but he also does not know how to loosen the tight grip of vigilance that has become his daily state.

Over time, he starts to feel detached from people around him. He is present at family gatherings but not fully there, as if part of him remains in that other place. He avoids crowded markets and dislikes being in unfamiliar buildings. He chooses familiar routes, familiar chairs, familiar routines. He keeps working because work gives shape to the day, though he is more fatigued now and notices his concentration slipping when he is tired or reminded of the captivity. He pushes through, telling himself he has survived worse, but the effort of holding himself together is constant.

In session, he presents as a man who has spent years carrying fear privately, almost as a duty. He speaks slowly about the captivity, with long pauses and occasional efforts to minimize what happened, yet his body tells the fuller story: the tightened jaw, the restless hands, the way he scans the room before settling. He remains devoted to his wife and family, but he lives with the persistent sense that the world can turn dangerous without warning, and that part of him is still listening for the sound of the door opening.
